topic: 限时写作：立场与充分论证
grammarFocus: 让步、条件、因果；复杂句和简单句的清楚组合。
title: 限时写作：立场与充分论证 · Four listening sections
instructions: 原创模拟训练材料；先独立作答，再核对依据。四节音频共40题，按顺序听音作答。合成训练音频时长不同于正式考试。
transcript:
Section 1: The Writing Workshop Debate

Mia: Hi, Tom. You look worried. What's up?
Tom: Oh, hi Mia. It's this timed writing task for our English class. We have to write an argument about whether students should be allowed to use AI tools for homework. I'm not sure how to structure it.
Mia: I see. Well, the key is to take a clear position and support it with reasons. Have you decided your stance?
Tom: I think so. I believe students should be allowed to use AI tools, but only if they use them responsibly. Although some teachers worry about cheating, I think AI can help students learn faster.
Mia: That's a reasonable position. But you need to acknowledge the other side. For example, if students rely too much on AI, they might not develop their own thinking skills.
Tom: Right. So I should include a concession? Like, 'Even though AI can be helpful, it should not replace the learning process'?
Mia: Exactly. And then you can follow with a condition: 'Provided that students use AI as a guide rather than a crutch, it can be beneficial.' That shows balance.
Tom: Okay, I like that. But how do I make my argument convincing? I mean, what kind of evidence should I use?
Mia: You could use examples from your own experience. For instance, if you used an AI tool to check your grammar, you can explain how it helped you improve. That's a personal example.
Tom: That makes sense. But I'm worried about the time limit. We only have 40 minutes to write the whole essay. How can I plan quickly?
Mia: Good question. First, spend five minutes planning your main argument and two supporting reasons. Then, write your introduction with a clear thesis statement. After that, write two body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence and evidence. Finally, write a conclusion that restates your position.
Tom: So, basically: plan, intro, two body paragraphs, conclusion. That's five parts. But what if I run out of time?
Mia: If you run out of time, make sure you at least finish your conclusion. A complete essay is better than an unfinished one. Also, keep your sentences clear. Mix simple sentences with complex ones. For example, use a simple sentence for your main point, and a complex sentence for your evidence.
Tom: Can you give me an example of a complex sentence with a concession?
Mia: Sure. 'Although AI tools can generate ideas quickly, students must still evaluate those ideas critically.' That's a complex sentence with a concession clause.
Tom: Nice. And what about cause and effect? How do I show that?
Mia: You can use words like 'because', 'therefore', or 'as a result'. For instance, 'Because students receive instant feedback from AI, they can correct their mistakes immediately.' That shows cause and effect.
Tom: Great. I feel more confident now. Thanks, Mia.
Mia: No problem. Just remember to stay within the word limit—around 250 words. And proofread if you have time.
Tom: I will. Thanks again!

Section 2: The Community Debate Workshop

Hello, and welcome to the Riverside Community Centre. My name is Sarah, and I'm the coordinator of the new Debate Workshop. I'm glad you're interested in joining us, so let me give you all the details you need. This workshop is for adults who want to improve their speaking and argument skills. It is designed for people who would like to express their opinions more clearly and confidently in everyday discussions as well as in formal debates. It starts on the 5th of March and runs for six weeks. Each session is on Tuesday evenings from 7 to 9 pm. The fee is 40 pounds for the whole course, but students and seniors pay only 25 pounds. You can pay online or at the front desk. Please register by the 1st of March so we can prepare materials. The workshop will be held in Room 12, on the second floor. There is a lift, but it is quite small, so please arrive early if you need it. Now, let me tell you what we will cover. In the first two weeks, we will focus on building clear arguments. You will learn how to state your position and support it with reasons and evidence. In weeks three and four, we will practise concession and counter-argument. That means you will learn to acknowledge the other side's point before explaining why you still disagree. This is a key skill in debates. In the final two weeks, we will put everything together in full debates. Each participant will have a chance to speak for three minutes, followed by questions from the audience. We will also discuss conditional and causal language, such as 'if... then...' and 'because... so...'. These structures help you connect ideas clearly. You don't need any previous debate experience. However, you should be comfortable speaking in front of others. If you are not sure, you can come to a free taster session on the 26th of February. Just email me at sarah@riverside.org to book a place. The taster is from 6 to 7 pm in the same room. One more thing: we will record the final debates for feedback purposes. If you do not want to be recorded, please let me know before the course starts. We respect your privacy. Also, there is no exam at the end. Instead, you will receive a certificate of participation if you attend at least five sessions. I think that's all. If you have questions, please call the centre on 01234 567890. Thank you.

Section 3: Timed Writing: Taking a Position and Arguing It Fully

Tutor: Today we're reviewing your forty-minute practice essays, especially clear positions and developed arguments. Mia, how did the time limit affect you?
Mia: I spent too long planning, so I only had about fifteen minutes to write. I supported banning cars from city centres because of pollution, but I gave only one example and didn't explain its significance.
Tutor: Leo, what concerned you?
Leo: I'm not sure my argument was fully developed. I supported free university education, but some of my complex sentences were hard to follow.
Tutor: You need a useful mix. Complex sentences show relationships, while simple sentences can make your main point stand out. For instance: 'Although free university would be expensive, it could increase social mobility.' Then a separate simple sentence: 'This benefit is long-term.'
Mia: So simple sentences aren't something to avoid?
Tutor: Exactly. You should also acknowledge a relevant counterargument before responding to it. Leo, did you consider the cost?
Leo: No. I explained how poorer students might benefit but left the cost out.
Tutor: You can refute a counterargument, accept part of it or qualify your position. For example: 'While the cost is high, the long-term economic benefits outweigh it.' That needs supporting explanation, not just an impressive connector. A concession shows that you've considered another side.
Mia: I used, 'If governments invest in public transport, then car use will decline.' Is that a useful conditional?
Tutor: Yes, for your proposed argument. For these practice essays, one or two well-placed conditionals are enough. There is no universal quota; use them when they clarify a relationship. For cause and effect, explain the mechanism rather than simply listing causes.
Leo: I could explain how reducing financial barriers allows more low-income students to attend, then how that could affect the workforce.
Tutor: Good. Make clear which outcomes are possible, rather than presenting every prediction as certain.
Mia: What time plan should I try next?
Tutor: Spend five minutes planning, thirty minutes writing, and five minutes checking. That's a plan for this forty-minute exercise, not a rule that guarantees a strong essay.
Mia: And where should the position appear?
Tutor: State it clearly in the introduction and return to it in the conclusion. Mia, your first sentence was a question: 'Should cars be banned?' That doesn't state your position. You could write, 'Cars should be banned from city centres because they cause pollution and congestion.'
Leo: Should I shorten my introduction too?
Tutor: Yes. You spent three sentences giving background. Keep the background brief—one or two sentences—then state your position.
Leo: So I should decide which supporting points and objections matter, rather than force every essay into one sequence?
Tutor: Precisely. The goal is to argue fully, not just to list points. Choose the structure that answers the actual question, and use sentence length to make that reasoning clear.

Section 4: The Art of the Timed Essay: Taking a Stand and Defending It

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about a skill that many of you will need in your academic writing: writing a timed essay in which you take a clear position and defend it convincingly. This is not just about writing quickly; it is about thinking clearly under pressure. In the next twenty minutes, I will discuss three key strategies: planning your argument, using concession and conditionals effectively, and combining complex and simple sentences for clarity. Let's begin.

First, planning. When you have only forty minutes to write an essay, you might be tempted to start writing immediately. However, I strongly advise you to spend the first five minutes planning. Why? Because a clear plan helps you avoid repetition and ensures that your argument is logical. Start by identifying the question type. Is it asking you to agree or disagree, discuss two views, or evaluate a problem? Once you know that, you can decide on your position. Your position is your main claim, and it should be stated clearly in the introduction. For example, if the question asks whether technology makes us more isolated, you might argue that it does not, provided that it is used wisely. Notice how I used a conditional there: 'provided that it is used wisely.' This qualifies your claim and shows that you are aware of complexities.

Now, let's move to concession. Concession means acknowledging the opposing view before you refute it. This makes your argument stronger because it shows you have considered other perspectives. A common way to concede is to use 'although' or 'while.' For instance, 'Although social media can connect people across distances, it can also create superficial relationships.' Here, you admit a benefit but then present a limitation. Another useful phrase is 'it is true that... but...' For example, 'It is true that online learning offers flexibility, but it often lacks face-to-face interaction.' Using concession effectively demonstrates critical thinking.

Next, conditionals. Conditionals are essential for expressing hypothetical situations and their consequences. The first conditional, with 'if' and the present tense, is used for real possibilities: 'If students manage their time well, they will feel less stressed.' The second conditional, with 'if' and the past tense, is for unreal or unlikely situations: 'If I had more time, I would research more thoroughly.' In timed essays, conditionals help you explore implications and propose solutions. However, be careful not to overuse them; too many conditionals can make your writing seem uncertain.

Finally, let's talk about sentence structure. A common mistake in timed essays is writing only long, complex sentences. While complex sentences are valuable for showing relationships between ideas, they can also confuse the reader if they are too long. On the other hand, short, simple sentences can be powerful for emphasis. For example, after a long explanation, you might write: 'This is a problem.' That short sentence draws attention. The key is to mix complex and simple sentences deliberately. Use complex sentences to explain causes and effects, and simple sentences to state your main points clearly.

To sum up, effective timed writing requires careful planning, strategic concession, appropriate conditionals, and a balanced mix of sentence types. Remember, it's not about writing the longest essay; it's about writing the clearest argument. With practice, you can master these skills. Thank you.

grammar.title: 让步、条件、因果：复杂句与简单句的组合
grammar.explanation: 在英语写作中，我们可以用简单句表达主要观点，用复杂句表达让步、条件或因果关系。让步常用although, even though, while等引导；条件常用if, provided that, unless等；因果常用because, since, therefore, as a result等。混合使用简单句和复杂句可以使文章清晰且有逻辑。
